chapter: New York dance halls and one-nighters
title: One-night stands, guarantees, handling the money, and the Memphis Five
summary: La Rocca describes touring one-nighters on guarantees plus percentages, counting the door, carrying cash in a money belt and splitting five ways. He then covers Robertson and Margie, replacing him with Signorelli, Shields leaving, and the Memphis Five.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Getting paid: wages, scale and the pay envelope

blocks.x: many of the places we had returning engagements. Through my files, you'll be able to see the office of jobs we had. And all the New Orleans boys was not working. And if I'd have had a thousand men that could play our music, I could have been a millionaire today because I had jobs for all of them. But there was none of them could fit the bill. In this one-night stands, we came back. And it was a tough job, riding all night to go to another place. For instance, you'd jump from Philadelphia to Pittsburgh. It was almost a whole 12-hour ride. Pennsylvania's a big state. It ain't like New Orleans or Baton Rouge. You can make it in a couple hours. But over there, you took a train. If you went by car, it would take you all day long. Maybe a day and a half to get there. So we used to go in on an $850 or $750 guarantee, plus 50% of the takeover over $800 some odd. I'd had a man stationed at the door with one of these little meters. The admission was $1.10 for ladies and women. When they went in there, each time one passed through the door, this man would click this little machine what he had in his pocket. The man in the office didn't know that we were keeping tab. At 11 o'clock, I'd come down and find out how much money we had. I wasn't worried about who coming after 11 o'clock. All I was worried about getting what I had coming to me at that time. And I didn't care if they let him in free after that. So we played in places like armrests. Some of these rubber-lipped men without electrical equipment, they couldn't be hooded. 50 feet. You had to have power and lungs made of steel to fill a place almost a half a square long and a square wide. Or a square long and a half a square wide. Either way you put it. And as many as 5,000 to 8,000 to 10,000 people would be in there jammed in there. They had alternate bands. They had 8,000, 10,000, 12 pieces would play on the opposite side of us. And when we played, everybody got to dance. When they played, nobody danced. Sometimes our shift would go for half an hour as long as they'd applaud. I'd stare there pouring at them because we wanted to come back. 11 o'clock, I'd go pick up this money like I told them. Check up with the men. Some men were honest. Some would try to cheat me. Well, I didn't mind if they beat me out of $100 because they had a little extra expense. We had nothing to put out. Just come there dry with our instruments. No music to carry. No sound equipment. No one to pay this man. If it was a question of $100, $150, I wouldn't open my mouth. When it comes to about $400 or $500, I'd squawk for my end of it. I'd take $400. I'd shove it in my pocket. I'd take the rest of it, whether it's $1,200 or $1,800. I had a money belt made that fit around my waist. And I'd take this money and shove it in my belt all around like that. None of the boys would walk with me. They're afraid that someone might hold me up and kill me. They'd run off. Some of them would stand around watching. But I had to go get a cab and ride to a hotel and hold that money in my possession all night until the bank opened the next morning that these boys could get money on us and send them to wherever they wanted to send them. This money was split five ways. I never got a dime extra outside of expenses like telegraphs. A different thing. It was a cooperating band. And everything I did was cooperative. Today, the boys said they kept books for me. But it's untrue. Because they're going to look through these papers and find out that they got the best break. I didn't get the best break. I did the work. I did the brain work. I composed all the numbers. I did everything in the band. I knew it was my only opportunity in life to make a success. I'm working for my boy. Fifteen years old. You'll know what it is when you see something in front of you that you can make money out of it. You're not going to let that opportunity pass you. And that was my motto. Opportunity to knock once. We came back to New York. We was tired. I went to wait and sign a contract for Sixty Bazzoni. I think that's S-I-X-T-I. He was a man that run a lot of dance schools. He must have been about eight or nine dancing ballaces around New York. I'm going to enter my story. After we finished his one night, Shields had given his notice that he intended to retire from the music dance. I had already changed the piano. I forgot to tell you that too. At the Follies Bouget. When Robertson failed to come through with his agreement, he was to give us a thousand dollars for the band for plugging Margie and making Margie a hit song. Up to this time, Robertson never had a hit. I'm all mixed up on this thing, but if you listen, you get these things, you'll be able to get them right. Right. And I plugged Margie and singing the blues and many other Robertson's numbers. And I was instrumental in getting this thing to be recorded by Victor in 1920. When Robertson got his first statement, they had sold about a million and a half records. He must have got about eight, nine thousand dollars of money for himself. There were three men interested in that. There were three of them who used to pay this money. And they reneged on it, a thousand dollars. That was... I can't think of the other man's name, but the names are on the song. You will see. Robertson was in the band. And now I gave Robertson his two weeks notice and replaced him with Frank Signorelli. At this time, Frank Signorelli and Johnny Costs and them had a little band. They called them Memphis Five. They were copies of what they copied off the original Big Slayer Jazz Band recordings and stuff. And this boy had not much time, but only go over a few little other numbers that he didn't know our arrangements on. In the afternoon, I got to play them openly, showing them different parts of where to make the break and all. And each night, we had a different number at all so it wouldn't be too hard for him to remember. And that was the band that we went to Atlantic City before we went on the one night stands. I tell you that too. It was here that they went with Sophie Tucker too. It was Bill Lewis, Sophie Tucker. Our building was in lights on the outside of the building. It remained there for a year after that we weren't playing there. There was Katz's place. I don't remember the name now, but if you look up my pieces of paper that's in there, you'll find the contract of Katz, the amount of money we got from him. And we got room and board with this contract that was agreed that we were to get room and board. Then we went on the one night stand. It was this time that Shields was getting too hard. Shields had already married before we went to London and his wife couldn't travel with him and he was away from his wife. And from this money he was making, almost $1,000 a week for about eight, nine weeks, he thought he was fat. This money would last him forever. I don't know where he went, whether he went to Chicago or California. I wouldn't know because I never corresponded with him. He didn't correspond with me. Now we go to the balconies, Jimmy Light Town, which played with Signorella in the Memphis Five when the first of all was a young boss in Brooklyn joined my band. After five weeks, I went down with Influenza. I pulled the band out rather than put substitutes in there. When I pulled the band out, that's when they formed the Memphis Five and brought them into the balconies. This is the beginning of the notoriety of the Memphis Five. He had learned the numbers and the arrangements by playing along with the original Dix-Solene Jazz Band, which I had taught this, Signorella, and Light Town. It was easy for them to have Mick Moore and her drummer sit in and play with them because that was the nucleus of their band. They had the two men right there. All they needed was the trombone and the drums to fill out their band. They made many records for Sam Lanham on the last Black Aces. Some of the arrangements they'd taken that Frank Signorelli won especially, and I wish I could shimmy like my sister Kate. Almond P. Ron in 1917 sent me this music and asked me if I could set this music for recording. I had never known P. Ron but I heard him play. He used to play most of all the white society dances. He and Robe Show, they had all the society dances. Very few white bands ever played for society. Always these two Negro bands. Now they played conventional ragtime music. The music of that era which was played by white men also.
